topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Simple vs compound interest calculations
topic.scope: SI = PRT, compound interest grows on interest too, amount vs interest, half-yearly and quarterly compounding, rate per period, depreciation and population growth, confusing amount with interest earned

nodes.name: Simple interest
external_prereqs: multiplication of whole numbers and decimals

nodes.name: Principal is the money borrowed or deposited at the start
Interest is only the extra money paid for use of principal
Rate of 8% p.a. means Rs 8 per Rs 100 each year
SI = P x R x T / 100 with T in years
In SI the interest is the same every year
In CI, interest is also earned on earlier interest
CI is greater than SI for more than one period
Amount after the first year becomes principal for the next year
Compounding half-yearly: rate is halved and periods doubled
Compounding quarterly: rate divided by 4, periods multiplied by 4
Time with a fraction of year, e.g. 2 1/2 years, needs period conversion
Depreciation: value falls by a percent of the current value each year

misconceptions.statement: The amount is the interest, so the total money returned is the interest.
misconceptions.why: Both words refer to money at the end, and the question says 'find the amount' loosely.
misconceptions.fix: Interest is only the extra money. Amount is the principal plus the interest.

probe.question: Rs 1000 is lent for 1 year and the interest is Rs 80. What is the interest?

misconceptions.root_belief: related words mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors in percentage and financial mathematics

misconceptions.statement: Amount means the money you first put in.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech 'amount of money' means any sum, such as the starting sum.
misconceptions.fix: Amount is what you get at the end: principal plus interest. The money you put in at the start is the principal.

probe.question: Rs 500 is deposited and earns Rs 50 interest. What is the amount?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: After finding SI, the answer to 'find the amount' is just the SI.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after the formula step and forget the last addition.
misconceptions.fix: The formula gives only interest. Add the principal to get the amount.

probe.question: P = Rs 2000, SI = Rs 300. Find the amount.

misconceptions.root_belief: the last computed number is the answer

misconceptions.statement: A rate of 8% means the interest is Rs 8 on any principal.
misconceptions.why: Students read 8% as the number 8 without the 'per hundred' meaning.
misconceptions.fix: 8% per year means Rs 8 on every Rs 100 each year, so Rs 800 earns Rs 64 in a year.

probe.question: How much interest does Rs 2000 earn in 1 year at 5% p.a.?

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol means just its face number

misconceptions.statement: In SI = PRT/100, time can be put in months directly.
misconceptions.why: The question gives the time in months and students plug in the number without converting.
misconceptions.fix: Rate is per year, so time must be in years. 6 months is 1/2 year.

probe.question: Find SI on Rs 1000 at 10% p.a. for 6 months.

misconceptions.root_belief: units do not matter, only the numbers
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies of unit errors in ratio and rate problems

misconceptions.statement: The SI formula is P x R x T without dividing by 100.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the product and forget that the rate is a percentage.
misconceptions.fix: Divide by 100 because the rate is per hundred: SI = PRT/100.

probe.question: Find SI on Rs 500 at 4% for 2 years.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule is remembered as a pattern without its meaning

misconceptions.statement: Simple interest grows bigger each year.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the idea from compound interest or from money growing in general.
misconceptions.fix: In SI, interest is always computed on the original principal, so it is the same every year.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10% SI. How much interest is earned in the 2nd year alone?

misconceptions.root_belief: growth always speeds up over time

misconceptions.statement: Compound interest is just the SI repeated, so it equals SI x number of years.
misconceptions.why: Students see the same word 'interest' and the same rate and apply the SI rule again.
misconceptions.fix: In CI, each year's interest is calculated on the new, larger amount, so it grows every year.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10% CI for 2 years: what is the interest?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student confusion between linear and exponential growth

misconceptions.statement: CI is greater than SI even for the first year.
misconceptions.why: Students assume compounding always gives more.
misconceptions.fix: For one period, CI and SI are equal. CI becomes larger only from the second period.

probe.question: Rs 2000 at 5% for 1 year: is CI more than SI?

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case holds in every case

misconceptions.statement: In CI, the interest of every year is calculated on the original principal.
misconceptions.why: Students keep using P in each step because the formula starts with P.
misconceptions.fix: Each year's interest is found on the amount at the end of the previous year.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10% CI: what is the interest for the 2nd year?

misconceptions.root_belief: the starting value stays the base forever
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student reasoning on compound growth

misconceptions.statement: A = P(1 + R/100)^n means multiply P(1 + R/100) by n.
misconceptions.why: Students read the exponent as multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: The power n means multiplying (1 + R/100) by itself n times, not by n.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10% CI for 2 years: find A using the formula.

misconceptions.root_belief: a power means multiply by the exponent
misconceptions.source_hint: research on exponent misconceptions in school algebra

misconceptions.statement: The bracket is (R/100), without adding 1.
misconceptions.why: Students forget that the amount includes the principal, not only the growth.
misconceptions.fix: The factor is 1 + R/100 because the principal stays and the interest is added.

probe.question: Find A for Rs 1000 at 10% for 1 year using the formula.

misconceptions.root_belief: the last computed number is the answer

misconceptions.statement: The compound amount formula gives the compound interest directly.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the result of the formula as the final answer.
misconceptions.fix: The formula gives the amount. Subtract the principal to get the CI.

probe.question: Rs 1000 becomes Rs 1210 by the formula. What is the CI?

misconceptions.root_belief: related words mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors in financial mathematics

misconceptions.statement: Half-yearly compounding means the rate stays the same and only the time is doubled.
misconceptions.why: Students change one quantity and forget the rate is per year.
misconceptions.fix: For half-yearly, halve the rate and double the number of periods.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10% p.a. compounded half-yearly for 1 year: what are R and n?

misconceptions.root_belief: change one thing and the rest stays

misconceptions.statement: Half-yearly compounding gives the same amount as yearly compounding.
misconceptions.why: Students think the total time and annual rate are all that matter.
misconceptions.fix: More frequent compounding gives interest on interest earlier, so the amount is slightly larger.

probe.question: Is the amount at 10% p.a. for 1 year the same, compounded yearly or half-yearly?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the total quantity matters, not how it is split

misconceptions.statement: Quarterly compounding means the rate is halved and periods are doubled.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the half-yearly steps without noticing a quarter is 3 months.
misconceptions.fix: A year has 4 quarters, so divide the rate by 4 and multiply the years by 4.

probe.question: For 8% p.a. compounded quarterly for 1 year, what are the rate per period and the number of periods?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: For 2 1/2 years compounded yearly, the formula can be used with n = 2.5 directly.
misconceptions.why: Students put the fraction into the exponent because it looks like any number.
misconceptions.fix: At class level, apply the formula for the 2 whole years and then SI for the half-year on that amount. Or compound half-yearly with n = 5.

probe.question: How do you find CI on Rs 1000 for 2 1/2 years at 10% p.a. compounded yearly?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: If a machine loses 10% of its value each year, it loses 10% of the original value every year.
misconceptions.why: Students link the percent to the original price, as in SI.
misconceptions.fix: Each year the loss is 10% of the value at the start of that year, so the loss gets smaller.

probe.question: A Rs 1000 machine depreciates 10% a year. What is its value after 2 years?

misconceptions.root_belief: the starting value stays the base forever
misconceptions.source_hint: research on successive percentage change errors

misconceptions.statement: Depreciation uses the same formula as growth, with (1 + R/100)^n.
misconceptions.why: Students memorise one formula and ignore the direction of change.
misconceptions.fix: For a decrease, the factor is (1 - R/100), so A = P(1 - R/100)^n.

probe.question: A Rs 1000 scooter depreciates 10% for 1 year. What is its value?

misconceptions.root_belief: one formula fits all situations

misconceptions.statement: Population growth of 5% a year adds the same number of people each year.
misconceptions.why: Students treat growth like a fixed addition, as in SI.
misconceptions.fix: Each year's increase is 5% of that year's population, so the number added grows.

probe.question: A town of 10000 grows 5% yearly. What is the population after 2 years?

misconceptions.root_belief: growth always adds a fixed amount
misconceptions.source_hint: research on linear vs exponential thinking in percentage growth

misconceptions.statement: Compound interest is a different, special kind of money, not related to the SI idea.
misconceptions.why: The two names and two formulas look unrelated.
misconceptions.fix: Both are interest on money. They differ only in whether earlier interest is added to the base for the next period.

probe.question: How does CI differ from SI?

misconceptions.root_belief: different names mean different things
